en_alt: There are a lot of photos on your phone.
There are many photographs on your phone.
note: Equally valid renderings of мно́го and фотогра́фий for the word-bank drill.

en_alt: What is your sister's name?
note: The commonest English rendering of Как зову́т…? should also be accepted.

en_alt: I saw your photos.
note: Photos/photographs are interchangeable here.

en_alt: I lack something important.
note: More literal rendering of не хвата́ет, still natural English.

en_alt: I want to say something to you.
note: Literal rendering of сказа́ть тебе́ is equally natural.

ru: На чём ты е́здишь на рабо́ту?
note: Literal but idiomatic English for the на чём + е́здить frame.

en_alt: What do they make cheese from?
note: The active impersonal-plural reading is the literal one and should be accepted.

en_alt: What is that?
note: э́то covers both this and that in a bare identifying question.

ru: Я живу́ в э́том до́ме уже́ год.
en_alt: I have been living in this house for a year now.
note: Progressive perfect is the equally natural rendering of the present + уже́.

en_alt: I gave a book to this boy.
note: Both English ditransitive orders are valid.

en_alt: Let's go to the cinema together.
note: Пойдём is a first-person-plural invitation; both readings are current English.

en_alt: Buy me some ice cream, please.
note: Mass-noun reading of моро́женое is equally valid.

en_alt: I am cold, close the window.
note: The Russian uses a comma; the comma-joined English should also be accepted.

en_alt: After the performance the guests applauded for a long time.
After the play the guests applauded for a long time.
note: спекта́кль is glossed 'play'; the alternatives track the gloss the learner is shown.

en_alt: Who are you applauding?
note: 'Who' is the ordinary modern English object form and should not be marked wrong.

ru: Е́сли бы бы́ли ули́ки, его́ бы арестова́ли.
en: If there had been evidence, they would have arrested him.
en_alt: If there were evidence, they would arrest him.
note: The two halves disagreed: a present counterfactual protasis ('if there were') with a past-counterfactual apodosis ('would have arrested'); the past reading fits the perfective better, so both halves now sit in the past.

en_alt: They arrested him yesterday evening.
He was arrested last night.
note: The Russian is an impersonal plural, so the active rendering is the literal one.

en_alt: He used to run every day before.
Earlier he ran every day.
note: Ра́ньше is unrendered in en_gb (it is carried by 'used to'); the alternatives spell it out.

en_alt: The children are running in the courtyard.
note: двор is glossed 'courtyard'; both are natural.

ru: Без трениро́вки я бы не бе́гал так бы́стро.
По утра́м я бе́гаю в па́рке.
С понеде́льника я бу́ду бе́гать по утра́м.
en_alt: From Monday I will be running in the mornings.
note: Uncontracted form for the word-bank drill.

ru: Мы бу́дем бежа́ть к фи́нишу ско́ро.
note: The Russian word order is off — a native would front the adverb («Ско́ро мы бу́дем бежа́ть к фи́нишу») or use the perfective побежи́м; the English is a faithful rendering of what is written.

en_alt: The children are running towards the river.
note: к with a goal renders as either 'to' or 'towards'.

ru: Е́сли бы я опа́здывал, я бы бежа́л.
en_alt: If I were running late, I would run.
note: опа́здывать is imperfective 'be running late'; both readings are natural.

en_alt: Where are you running?
note: The stranded 'to' is optional in English.

ru: С ва́ми я охо́тно бесе́довала бы до́льше.
en_alt: I would gladly have talked with you for longer.
note: бы + past covers both the present and the past counterfactual reading.

ru: По́сле ле́кции студе́нты бу́дут бесе́довать с а́втором.
en_alt: After the lecture the students will talk with the author.
note: с renders as 'with' as readily as 'to'.

en_alt: We are talking about the weather.
note: Matches the 'talk' rendering used by the word's other examples.

en: Do you talk in the evening?
en_alt: Do you converse in the evening?
note: 'Do you converse…' reads as translationese and is out of step with the 'talk/chat' rendering used by this word's other examples; the old wording is kept as an alt.

ru: Без но́востей я бы беспоко́илась ещё бо́льше.

en_alt: Don't worry, everything will be all right.
note: хорошо́ renders as 'fine' or 'all right' equally.

en_alt: I worry about you.
I am worried for you.
note: беспоко́иться за takes both 'about' and 'for' in English.

en_alt: Are you worried about your health?
note: Stative rendering is equally natural.

en_alt: Mum is worried about her son.
note: Both the habitual and the stative reading fit the present tense here.

en_alt: Are you worried about your son?
note: Stative rendering is equally natural.

ru: Ма́ма беспоко́илась о́бо мне всю ночь.
note: The stress mark looks wrong: in обо мне the stress falls on мне, and the same word is written unstressed elsewhere in the corpus («Он всегда́ ду́мает обо мне.»); the English is correct.

en_alt: He was kicking the ball with his foot.
He struck the ball with his foot.
note: бил is imperfective, so the progressive reading should also be accepted.

ru: За́втра часы́ бу́дут бить ка́ждый час.
На его́ ме́сте я бы не бил ребёнка.
en_alt: If I were him, I would not hit a child.
note: Idiomatic equivalent of на его́ ме́сте.
The English is right, but the headword gloss 'to fight' does not cover the 'beat/pound against' sense the sentence needs — the gloss is probably the half to widen.
Same as the waves example: 'beat' (of a heart) is not covered by the gloss 'to fight'.

ru: Без наде́жды никто́ бы не би́лся так до́лго.
en_alt: Without hope nobody would fight so long.
note: nobody/no one are interchangeable.

ru: За тако́й шанс она́ благодари́ла бы судьбу́ всю жизнь.
en_alt: For such a chance she would thank fate all her life.
note: The literal word order tracks the Russian and should be accepted.
Frame collision only: the partner sentence is an infinitive after 'I want to', so the imperative here is still distinguishable.

ru: По́сле конце́рта она́ бу́дет благодари́ть всех ли́чно.
en: After the concert she will be thanking everyone in person.
en_alt: After the concert she will thank everyone in person.
note: бу́дет благодари́ть is the imperfective future; the progressive marks that and clears the 'will thank' frame collision with the perfective поблагодари́шь.
Frame collision only: the partner reads 'I want to thank you', which the drill can still tell apart.
Frame collision only; the partner sentence differs in subject and object throughout.

en_alt: She used to thank the teacher.
note: Identical collision with the perfective «Она́ поблагодари́ла учи́теля.» = 'She thanked the teacher'; the imperfective past is fixed here so the perfective keeps the single-completed-event reading.

en_alt: The child has been ill for a week now.
note: Renders уже́ explicitly.

en_alt: In winter children often get ill.
note: Matches the 'get ill' rendering used by this word's other examples.

en_alt: Please don't fall ill!
Please stay well!
note: 'Don't be ill' is not something an English speaker says; the negated imperative of боле́ть is 'don't get ill'.

ru: Без тёплой оде́жды ты бу́дешь боле́ть.
en_alt: Without warm clothes you will get ill.
note: Inceptive reading of the imperfective future is equally natural.

en_alt: Do you get ill often?
note: Matches the sibling examples' rendering.

ru: Всю доро́гу мы бу́дем болта́ть обо всём.
en_alt: We will chat about everything the whole way.
note: Literal rendering of всю доро́гу, which is the more common English phrasing.

en_alt: The friends are chatting on the telephone.
note: телефо́н is glossed 'telephone'.

en_alt: Don't chat in the lesson!
note: уро́к is glossed 'lesson' and the headword gloss is 'to chat'.

ru: В библиоте́ке ты бы не болта́ла так гро́мко.
Во сне он бу́дет бормота́ть стра́нные слова́.
en: In his sleep he will be muttering strange words.
en_alt: In his sleep he will mutter strange words.
note: бу́дет бормота́ть is the imperfective future; the progressive marks the ongoing reading and clears three 'will mutter' frame collisions with пробормота́ть.

en_alt: The old man mutters something to himself.
note: Simple present is equally valid for the Russian present.

en_alt: I am muttering the words of a prayer.
note: Progressive reading of the Russian present is equally valid.

ru: От уста́лости я бы то́лько бормота́л.
note: Frame collision only, and the imperfective is the side that correctly reads 'would mutter'; the perfective partner is the half that should become 'would have muttered'.

en_alt: I am struggling with sleep.
note: боро́ться с renders as 'with' as readily as 'against'.

ru: Е́сли бы не тра́вма, он боро́лся бы за пе́рвое ме́сто.
en_alt: If not for the injury, he would be fighting for first place.
note: The imperfective supports the progressive reading too.

ru: Мы бу́дем боро́ться за свои́ права́ до конца́.
en_alt: We will fight for our rights to the end.
note: fight/struggle are both standard for боро́ться за.

en_alt: They are struggling for freedom.
note: Tracks the headword gloss 'to struggle'.

en_alt: Are you struggling for freedom?
note: Tracks the headword gloss 'to struggle'.

en_alt: The people fought for their rights.
note: fight/struggle interchangeable here.

ru: Без тебя́ я бы боя́лся идти́ домо́й оди́н.
en_alt: Without you I would be afraid to go home alone.
note: идти́ is glossed 'to go'.

en_alt: The little child is afraid of the dark.
note: small/little are interchangeable for ма́ленький.

en_alt: The dog was afraid of the thunder.
note: Article choice is free here.

en_alt: Are you taking an umbrella for the journey?
note: доро́га is glossed 'road/journey'; both renderings are natural.

en_alt: She borrowed books from the library.
She used to take books out of the library.
note: The imperfective past supports both the habitual and the plain past reading.

ru: Для рабо́ты она́ брала́ бы кни́ги в библиоте́ке.
en_alt: For work she would borrow books from the library.
note: Fronted adverbial matches the Russian order.

en_alt: Don't take the phone to school.
note: The Russian has no possessive; the article-only reading should be accepted.

en_alt: I take the book from the table.
note: Simple present is equally valid for the Russian present.

ru: С о́сени она́ бу́дет брать уро́ки му́зыки.

note: Frame collision only: the perfective partner is a different sentence about an umbrella, so the drill still has a cue.

en_alt: Are you joining hands?
Are you taking hold of each other's hands?
note: бра́ться за ру́ки is the inceptive 'join hands'; the alts stop the drill rejecting it.

en_alt: We join hands.
We take hold of each other's hands.
note: Same idiom as the вы sentence.

A native would use the perfective «Отку́да взяла́сь э́та иде́я?» here — the imperfective бралась forces a repeated reading that the past-simple English does not match — and the 'come from' sense is not covered by the gloss 'to take hold of'.

ru: Вы бы бра́лись за э́то без по́мощи?
Кто бу́дет бра́ться за э́ту рабо́ту?
note: Frame collision only; the partner sentence differs in subject and object, and 'will be taking on' would be awkward here.

en_alt: He is taking on difficult work.
note: Progressive reading of the Russian present is equally valid.

en_alt: I don't like shaving.
note: Gerund is at least as natural in English.

ru: На ва́шем ме́сте я бы не броса́ла му́сор на зе́млю.
en: In your place I would not throw rubbish on the ground.
en_alt: If I were you, I would not drop litter on the ground.
note: 'drop litter' replaced броса́ть/му́сор with a British idiom and 'if I were you' replaced на ва́шем ме́сте; the literal rendering is natural English and matches how the sibling «Не броса́й му́сор…» is translated.

ru: За́втра де́ти бу́дут броса́ть мяч во дворе́.
en_alt: Tomorrow the children will be throwing the ball in the courtyard.
note: двор is glossed 'courtyard'.

en_alt: The boy is throwing stones into the water.
note: Progressive reading of the Russian present is equally valid.

en_alt: Don't throw rubbish in the street!
note: British English prefers 'in the street'.
